key_insight: Multi-agent systems are not universally better than single-agent systems. The paper argues that their advantage depends on how information is distributed and bottlenecked across isolated local contexts versus one shared reasoning trace.
problem_solved: This paper addresses the unclear and inconsistent performance gap between multi-agent systems and single-agent systems on complex tasks, asking when splitting reasoning across multiple agents actually helps.
method: Apply an information bottleneck perspective to compare how single-agent systems and multi-agent systems store, transform, and pass reasoning information.
Characterize a single-agent system as accumulating the full reasoning trace in one shared context, while a multi-agent system relies on separate local contexts connected by limited communication.
Use this framework to explain when distributed reasoning improves performance and when communication constraints can hinder it.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this gives a principled way to decide whether to use a multi-agent setup instead of a single model. It can guide system design by matching task structure to the right reasoning architecture.
visual_elements: Side-by-side diagram of SAS vs. MAS context flow

Flowchart of task types where MAS helps versus hurts

paper_title: When Do Multi-Agent Systems Help? An Information Bottleneck Perspective
paper_authors: Wendi Yu, Lianhao Zhou, Xiangjue Dong, Sai Sudarshan Barath, Declan Staunton
